channel.title: Oleksandr Shepotylo
channel.description: When allies coerce, markets fragment, and geopolitics rewrites the trade map.

item.title: The Return of Protectionism: Trump’s 2025 Tariffs and the Shifting Landscape of Global Trade
item.description:
Donald Trump’s return to the presidency in 2025 triggered the most significant protectionist surge since the 1930s, with the US average effective tariff reaching 18.2% by August 2025 — the highest level in 90 years. We synthesise economic theory and empirical evidence on the welfare effects of the new tariffs, analyse the current US trade measures, and quantify their impacts using a structural gravity model. Beyond the direct cost of the duties themselves, ongoing tariff uncertainty disrupts firms’ planning, forces costly duplication of supply chains, and triggers capital flight that undermines the very industrial goals protectionism claims to serve.

Published in: LSE Public Policy Review, 2026. With Jun Du and Yujie Shi.

item.title: Beyond security: The trade implications of joining NATO
item.description:
Combining structural gravity methods with a staggered difference-in-differences design, we identify the causal effect of NATO membership on bilateral trade flows, separating it from the effect of a generic military alliance. NATO accession raises exports, with benefits that unfold gradually and intensify over time, coming through several channels: protecting and securing trade routes, lowering uncertainty and boosting cross-member investment, direct trade in military and military-related goods, and logistical support for military activity.

Working paper: SSRN Working Paper / BOFIT Discussion Paper, 2026. With Karen Jackson.

item.title: Political alliances and trade: Europe in a polarized world
item.description:
Bilateral trade flows increasingly track political alignment, not just the standard gravity-model fundamentals of distance, size, and trade agreements. Using a structural gravity framework, we show that political alliances are a statistically significant predictor of trade between European economies and the rest of the world, and that the strength of this relationship has grown as global politics has polarized.

Published in: European Journal of Political Economy, 85(C)

item.title: Transforming East Asia: Regional Integration in a Trade War Era
item.description:
As US–China trade tensions escalated, East Asian economies deepened regional integration with each other rather than retreating into protectionism. We document this shift in trade patterns and ask whether it reflects deliberate diversification away from exposure to the US–China relationship, or simply the mechanical effect of existing regional trade agreements taking fuller effect.

Published in: Open Economies Review, 34(3), 657–672

item.title: Non-tariff measures and productivity of Ukrainian food-processing firms
item.description:
Non-tariff measures imposed by trading partners act as a quality filter on Ukrainian food-processing exporters: firms that clear them see productivity gains, while the compliance costs push less productive firms out of export markets entirely. Using firm-level microdata, we separate this selection effect from the direct within-firm productivity effect of meeting stricter standards — evidence directly relevant to Ukraine’s ongoing agrifood market access negotiations with the EU.

Published in: Journal of Agricultural Economics, 73(1), 234–256

item.title: Belt and road: The China dream?
item.description:
We assess whether participation in China’s Belt and Road Initiative has delivered the trade gains its member countries were promised, using a structural gravity model to separate the initiative’s effect from underlying trends already under way before countries signed on.

Published in: China Economic Review, 67(C)

item.title: An examination of EU trade disintegration scenarios
item.description:
Using a structural gravity approach, we examine the welfare implications of scenarios in which the EU itself partially disintegrates, rather than just the UK leaving it. The remaining EU countries stand to lose considerably more from EU disintegration than they did from a disorderly Brexit. Some neighbouring high- and middle-income countries — Bosnia and Herzegovina and Norway among them — would actually benefit under certain disintegration scenarios, gaining trade competitiveness relative to the weakened EU bloc.

Published in: The World Economy, 2021. With Karen Jackson.

item.title: Popular Support For Trade Agreements And Partner Country Characteristics
item.description:
Public support for a trade agreement depends not just on its expected economic effects but on characteristics of the partner country — including factors with no direct bearing on trade volumes, such as perceived political alignment and cultural distance. We use survey experiments to separate economic from non-economic drivers of trade-agreement support, with direct implications for how governments should sequence and communicate new trade deals.

Published in: Economic Inquiry, 59(1), 549–566

item.title: Trade Wars: Are Good and Easy to Win?
item.description:
Taking its title from a well-known 2018 tweet, this paper uses a structural gravity approach to evaluate the welfare implications of US protectionist trade policy under three retaliatory scenarios from the EU and China. The impact on the US is negative under every scenario, ranging from 0.25% to 1.4% of GDP, with smaller US losses precisely when the EU and China do not retaliate — meaning it is a dominant strategy for both the EU and China to hold their tariffs against US goods at existing levels rather than de-escalate.

Working paper: SSRN Working Paper, 2018. With Karen Jackson.
